title: The Three Pillars
description: Learn the three pillars of observability — logs, metrics, and traces — and how SLIs and SLOs turn raw signals into actionable alerts.

segments.text: Imagine driving a car with no dashboard — no speedometer, no fuel gauge, no warning lights. That's what running a production system without observability feels like. Let's fix that.

Here's your system in production. Users are hitting it, but you can't see what's happening inside. Is it healthy? Slow? Erroring? You have no idea until users start complaining. By then, it's too late.

The first pillar is logs. Every event your application produces — requests handled, errors thrown, decisions made — gets written as a log entry. But not just any logs. Structured logs with consistent fields like timestamp, severity, request ID, and user ID.

Structured logs are searchable and parseable. Instead of grepping through walls of text, you can query: 'Show me all errors for user 42 in the last hour.' That's the difference between a haystack and a filing cabinet.
segments.thought_prompt: Why is structured logging (JSON) better than plain text log lines for debugging?

segments.text: The second pillar is metrics — numerical measurements over time. Counters track totals (requests served). Gauges track current values (CPU usage). Histograms track distributions (response time buckets). These power your dashboards.

Here's a crucial insight: averages lie. If your average response time is 100ms, it might mean most requests take 50ms but some take 2 seconds. Use percentiles instead. P99 tells you what the slowest 1% of users experience — that's where the pain lives.

The third pillar is distributed tracing. A single user request might hit your API gateway, then the auth service, then the orders service, then the database. A trace follows that entire journey, showing time spent at each hop.

Each step in a trace is called a span. Spans have a start time, duration, and metadata. Together they form a waterfall diagram that shows you exactly where time is being spent — and where the bottleneck hides.

Data without action is just noise. Alerting turns your observability signals into wake-up calls. But alert on symptoms, not causes. Alert on 'error rate exceeds 5%', not on 'CPU is at 80%' — high CPU might be perfectly fine.
segments.thought_prompt: What's the risk of alerting on too many things? How would you prioritize?

segments.text: This is where SLIs and SLOs come in. An SLI (Service Level Indicator) is a measurement — like the percentage of requests under 200ms. An SLO (Service Level Objective) is your target — 'we aim for 99.9% of requests under 200ms.'

The gap between 100% and your SLO is your error budget. A 99.9% SLO means you can afford 0.1% errors — about 43 minutes of downtime per month. When the budget runs low, freeze features and fix reliability. When it's healthy, ship fast.

So the three pillars: logs tell you WHAT happened, metrics tell you HOW MUCH is happening, traces tell you WHERE time is spent. Together with SLOs and alerting, they give you the dashboard to drive your system confidently.
